newsitem.title: CANADA: INTERVIEW - Arakis sees Sudan project safe.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Arakis sees Sudan project safe.

text.p: Canada's Arakis Energy Corp takes seriously threats of attack on its Sudanese oil operations made last week by a rebel leader but believes the region is protected from hostilities, Arakis chief executive John Mcleod said on Tuesday.
"We always take them seriously," Mcleod said in an interview. "Our reading right now is the area is secure and we'd like to keep it that way."

In an interview published Friday in Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat, Sudanese rebel leader Colonel John Garang warned Arakis that his forces would stike if needed to halt attempts to develop its oil concessions in Southern Sudan.

Garang, head of the Sudan People Liberation Army, said that if Arakis succeeded in extracting the oil in its Heglig and Unity fields, the Khartoum government would receive more money to use as funding in the 13-year Sudanese civil war.
"But we will not allow this to happen and we will strike at these operations," Garang was quoted as saying.
The SPLA is the largest and oldest southern Sudanese rebel group fighting for greater independence for the mainly Christian and animist south from the Moslem, Arabised north.
McLeod said the Sudan military continues to provide protection to Arakis. The firm also employs its own security and safety coordinators which work as go-betweens for the company and army.

He said, however, that recent speculation that Arakis had hired private South African mercenary company Executive Outcomes was false. "I've never talked to Executive Outcomes. There's no truth to that whatsoever."

An official with the Sudan Working Group, a Washington-based organization of humanitarian and multi-denominational religious groups, said Arakis's more immediate rebel concern would come from the South Sudan Independence Movement (SSIM), which controls the region closest to Arakis's oil fields.

The SSIM, which has frequently fought against the SPLA, in April signed a political charter with the Khartoum government, said Bill Lowrey, a Presbyterian clergyman who works with the Washington organization which strongly opposes the Arakis deal.
The SSIM has also observed a ceasefire since before the charter was signed.

"That charter is not a peace agreement, but it is a statement of principles that are supposed to be the basis for negotiating the peace agreement," Lowrey said. "Some other groups in addition to SSIM have signed that, but the mainstream SPLA have not."

Arakis has attempted for over a year to strike a joint venture deal to develop the fields, which harbor reserves currently estimated at about 600 million barrels, and build a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea from the concession.

Although the SPLA lacks control of the areas near the oil fields, a pipeline of the magnitude envisaged by Arakis, which would nearly span the country, could be threatened by the rebel group, Dowrey said.

McLeod has said Arakis was close to a deal with more than three international firms and set a target for the end of 1996 to make an announcement. He said Tuesday the company had meetings two weeks ago in Khartoum with prospective deal participants.
The United States government earlier this year included udan on a list of nations named under its anti-terrorist law.

However, apart from a stipulation that U.S. citizens or companies cannot receive funds from the Khartoum government, its oil companies are not barred from becoming participants in a deal with Arakis, according to legal interpretations of the legislation.
McLeod has declined to comment on whether U.S. oil company Occidental Petroleum Corp was examining entering a joint venture, as stock market players have speculated.

The U.S. State Department has told Reuters that Oxy was one of several U.S. companies that inquired for over a year about the potential ramifications of working in Sudan. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
